items.label: The world systems compared in print: Ursus 1588 and Roeslin 1597
items.description: Ursus's Fundamentum astronomicum (Strasbourg, end of July 1588) carried a planetary diagram equivalent in its geometry to Wittich's ‘sphere of revolutions’ of 1578, with the Earth turning daily, and appeared within months of Tycho's De mundi (Westman 2011, p. 293). Helisaeus Roeslin's De opere Dei creationis (Frankfurt 1597) was the first book to set the competing arrangements side by side, each as numbered propositions with a woodcut plate — Ptolemy, Copernicus, Ursus, Tycho and Roeslin's own — and the plates were mislabelled by the Frankfurt publisher: the Copernican system stands under Tycho's name with a printed apology beneath, Ursus's diagram under Copernicus's, Tycho's under Ursus's (pp. 342–347, figs 70–72; p. 574 n. 40, which also notes that Ursus in 1597 ‘shifted his position toward that of Tycho and accepted the intersection of the paths of Mars and the Sun’). Roeslin had borrowed Maestlin's copy of De mundi for two weeks at the end of 1588 and concluded that Ursus, Tycho's pupil, had taken the arrangement and added the Earth's daily motion so as not to seem to agree with him: ‘iudico Raymarum sua habere a Tychone (cuius discipulus fuit) et terram ille mobilem statuit, ne videatur cum Tychone consentire’ (Württembergische Landesbibliothek, Cod. Math. 4° 14b, fol. 19r; Granada 1996, pp. 119–120, as quoted by Westman, p. 566 n. 58); he also doubted that any astronomer had seen Mars's parallax exceed the Sun's (p. 342). The Frankfurt spring catalogue of 1597 announced Kepler's Mysterium, Tycho's Epistolae astronomicae and Roeslin's De opere Dei together (Fabian, Die Messkataloge des sechzehnten Jahrhunderts V, pp. 370, 372, 373; p. 573 n. 25); Ursus's reply, De astronomicis hypothesibus (Prague 1597), built on passages of the Epistolae, called Tycho ‘a mere mechanic’ and Rothmann ‘Rotzmann’ (p. 348). For the suit that followed, see the quarrel with Ursus.

items.label: Gilbert answers Tycho's cannon: De magnete (1600) and De mundo (1651)
items.description: In De magnete (London 1600), book VI, William Gilbert rebutted the thought experiment Tycho had set against the Earth's daily rotation in De mundi — the cannon fired east and west — and concluded that the diurnal motion ‘is not at all refuted by the illustrious Tycho Brahe through such arguments as these’ (De magnete, p. 341; Westman 2011, pp. 370–372, fig. 73 and p. 580 nn. 145–146). Gilbert knew Ursus's Fundamentum and Tycho's De mundi but shows no acquaintance with the Epistolae astronomicae or with the quarrel of 1597, and he did not, it seems, take Mars's parallax on Tycho's authority (p. 372 and n. 154). The posthumous De mundo nostro sublunari (Amsterdam 1651) describes the Tychonic ordering: ‘Illustrissimus Tycho Brahe Solem vult centrum esse secundorum mobilium, sive planetarum, terram vero constituit centrum universi; Mercurium & Venerem Copernici ratione circa Solem cieri’ (ed. 1965, p. 192; p. 580 n. 147). There is no evidence that Tycho saw De magnete before his death in 1601; Kepler had his copy by November 1602 and read Gilbert as the answer to the cannon (p. 372 and n. 159). Galileo's copy, with his provenance, is Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze B.R.121 (fig. 74, p. 373).

items.label: The fluid heaven in English: Heydon's Defence of Judiciall Astrologie (1603)
items.description: Sir Christopher Heydon's Defence of Judiciall Astrologie (Cambridge 1603), written against John Chamber, takes its astronomy from the Epistolae astronomicae and the Progymnasmata: ‘our modern Mathematickes’ had proved ‘but one onely continued substance from the concaue superficies of the Moone, to the 8. Sphere’, ‘as both Tycho Brahe and Rothmann, doe at large prouue: and therefore in his Progymnasmata deuiseth newe Hypotheses, quite differing from the olde’, with Rheticus, Ramus, Scultetus, Frischlin, Ursus, Aslakssøn and Fracastoro concurring (Heydon 1603, pp. 370–371, quoted by Westman 2011, p. 410 and p. 586 nn. 43–44). Heydon left the world system undecided — ‘whether they be (as Tycho would have it) but one continued orbe, or many, or whether (as Copernicus saith) the Sun be the center of the world’ — an agnosticism Westman relates to Ursus's scepticism about hypotheses; Bowden (1974, pp. 135–136) notes the inconsistencies of Heydon's use of Brahe and Kepler (p. 586 n. 42). It is the earliest English printing of Tycho's fluid heaven and of the Progymnasmata's ‘newe Hypotheses’, two years after his death.

items.label: The Tychonic hypothesis among the moderns, 1644–1674: Descartes, Wilkins, Wing, Hooke
items.description: Descartes's Principia philosophiae (Amsterdam 1644) sets the Tychonic hypothesis beside the Copernican and claims to ‘deny the motion of the Earth more carefully than Copernicus and more truthfully than Tycho’; from the vortices he deduces ‘the physical impossibility of the Sun's carrying with it all the planets except the Earth’, and of the comet observers, Tycho among them, he writes that ‘they did not dare to attribute to them the altitude which their calculations were revealing’ (Westman 2011, pp. 497–498 and p. 600 nn. 75–78). Wilkins, in the Discourse concerning a New Planet (1640), explained Tycho's resistance to Copernicus by the rule that ‘Every Man is naturally more affected to his own Brood, than to that of which another is the Author’ (p. 498 n. 84). Vincent Wing built his first compendium on ‘the tables of Tycho, Argoli, and Lansbergen’ and by 1669 dismissed Tycho's hypotyposis as ‘more ingenuous than true’ (p. 503 nn. 112, 116); Gassendi adhered, ‘at least outwardly’, to the Tychonic arrangement (p. 500 n. 91); Riccioli taught the semi-Tychonic at Parma (p. 499 n. 89; see the afterlife of the world-system). Hooke's Attempt to Prove the Motion of the Earth (London 1674) framed the stellar parallax as ‘an experimentum crucis to determine between the Tychonick and Copernican Hypotheses’, asked whether there was not ‘much reason for the Hypothesis of Ticho at least, when he with all the accurateness that he arrived to with his vast Instruments, or Riccioli, who pretends much to out-strip him, were not able to find any sensible Parallax of the Earths Orb among the fixt Stars’, and proposed a telescope better than their instruments (pp. 508–509 and nn. 140–143). Westman's gloss: the naked eye cannot distinguish an angle of less than a minute, so ‘Tycho and Riccioli thus claimed more than they could deliver’ (p. 509).

sources.label: The 2010 exhumation project (Aarhus University with the National Museum, Prague)

sources.contributes: The 1901 examination step by step: the dates, who was present, the state of the vault, the two skeletons and their dress, the measurements, the nasal fragment and its stain, Matiegka's five conclusions, the sealing of the skull fragment and the reburial.

sources.label: Matiegka, Bericht über die Untersuchung der Gebeine Tycho Brahe's (Prague, 1901)
sources.full: Heinrich (Jindřich) Matiegka, Bericht über die Untersuchung der Gebeine Tycho Brahe's. Erstattet von Dr. Heinrich Matiegka. Mit 2 Textfiguren. Vorgelegt den 11. Oktober 1901 in der Sitzung der königl. böhm. Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften (Prag: Verlag der königl. böhmischen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften, in Commission bei Fr. Řivnáč, 1901; printed by Dr. Ed. Grégr), 14 pp., two halftone Textfiguren of the facial fragment — the primary report of the opening of 24 June 1901 and the examination of 26–27 June. Cited as printed p. N (scan N); the title, its verso and the opening leaf are unnumbered (scans 1–3), the head-numbers run 4–14.
sources.contributes: The primary record of the 1901 examination, read at the page: the committee and the council, the commission, the vault and the two coffins, the measures (stature, the long-bone table after Manouvrier, the orbit, upper-face and nasal measures, the woman's 155 cm and skull measures), the moustache and hair, the six Gründe, the custody from the sacristy box to the sealed glass and the tin coffin, and the clothing samples given to the municipal museum.

sources.label: Hadravová, Hadrava & Shackelford, Instruments of the Renewed Astronomy (1996)
sources.full: Alena Hadravová, Petr Hadrava & Jole R. Shackelford (eds.), Tycho Brahe: Instruments of the Renewed Astronomy. English translation (Raeder et al. 1946) revised and commented (Praha: KLP – Koniasch Latin Press, 1996; Clavis monumentorum litterarum, Regnum Bohemiae 2, Facsimilia – Translationes 1), xv + 175 pp. The English volume of the 450th-anniversary set (with a colour facsimile of the Křivoklát copy and a complete Czech translation): Ræder's 1946 translation revised for fidelity to the Latin, the preface to Rudolf II translated for the first time, and 301 notes — philological, astronomical (Hadrava), biographical and classical — cross-referred to Opera omnia.
sources.contributes: The Mechanica's editions and translations as its Prologue recounts them, and the 450th-anniversary edition itself; the Hipparcos 'Tycho' catalogue named in the anniversary year (p. x, n. 4).

sources.full: József Jankovics & István Monok, Dudith András könyvtára. Részleges rekonstrukció / András Dudith's Library. sources.contributes: the entry that places Dudith's De mundi at the Royal Library and describes its annotation; the D-number system, the red ink Dudith preferred, his habit of keywording paragraphs in the margin, and the three roads of his books (Dietrichstein–Christina; Dresden; Hartenfels)

sources.label: Gingerich & Westman, The Wittich Connection (1988)
sources.full: Owen Gingerich and Robert S. Westman, The Wittich Connection: Conflict and Priority in Late Sixteenth-Century Cosmology (Transactions of the American Philosophical Society 78, part 7; Philadelphia, 1988).
sources.contributes: the Ursus affair narrated from Tycho's letters of 1588–1592 and from Ursus's and Kepler's texts, with the Wittich connection and the chronology of 1584–1587

sources.label: Westman, The Copernican Question (2011)
sources.full: Robert S. Westman, The Copernican Question: Prognostication, Skepticism, and Celestial Order (Berkeley and Los Angeles: University of California Press, 2011; first paperback printing 2020). Chapters 8, 10, 12–14 and 16–18 and the Conclusion for Tycho's readers and critics from Bruno to Hooke.
sources.contributes: Bruno's knowledge of Uraniborg and the route of the Acrotismus; Roeslin's mislabelled plates of 1597 and Ursus's two schemes; Gilbert's rebuttal of the cannon experiment; Heydon's English Progymnasmata; the Tychonic hypothesis among Descartes, Wilkins, Wing and Hooke — each with the primary text quoted and its page.

sources.label: Gilbert, De magnete (1600)
sources.full: William Gilbert, De magnete, magneticisque corporibus, et de magno magnete tellure physiologia nova (London: Peter Short, 1600), book VI; and De mundo nostro sublunari philosophia nova (Amsterdam 1651), ed. 1965. Cited at the page through Westman 2011, pp. 370–372 and p. 580 nn. 145–147.
sources.contributes: The first printed rebuttal of Tycho's argument from the cannon against the Earth's daily rotation, and the posthumous description of the Tychonic ordering.

sources.label: Opera omnia XIV (1929) — the letters and acts of the heirs
sources.full: Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, ed. J. L. E. Dreyer, vol. XIV: Epistolae et acta ad vitam Tychonis Brahe pertinentia (Copenhagen, 1929): nos. 284–285, Georg Brahe to Kepler, Prague 14 April 1627, and Kepler to the brothers Brahe, Ulm 20 April 1627, pp. 292–294.
sources.contributes: the terminal inventory of the Mechanica's blocks and plates: ten instrument blocks, the Uraniborg and Stjerneborg blocks and the Astronomia emblem in Prague in 1627, the loan to Hülsius remembered without a document, the portrait copperplate believed in a chest in the country, and Kepler's reply that the Tables did not need them

threads.gloss: The observations and their editions — how the numbers travelled: the inheritance, the archive, the first printing, the critical edition.
The astronomy that used him — the laws, the tables, the world-system, the instrumental method, and the data still worked today.
The objects that carry his name or his star: the crater, the supernova remnant, the globes that mapped Hven's sky, the signs read in the heavens.
The estate, the institutions and the grave — what became of his foundation, his money, his instruments' images and his body.
How his life and character were written, from the earliest contemporary verse and verdict to the modern editions.

The place itself after 1597 — the buildings as ruin, quarry, excavation and museum. Where the other threads follow what was made of Tycho's work, this one follows what became of the ground it was done on, and how it was recovered.

grades.A: Verified against the cited source itself — the primary print or manuscript, or a scholarly study held in the compilation's own library and read at the cited page.
grades.B: Reported: the claim rests on a secondary summary, on a study the compilation has not itself inspected, on a single partisan witness, or is an interpretive reading — stated as the source states it, and not independently confirmed.
grades.C: Entered on a record alone: the object or usage exists and the museum's or catalogue's record of it is cited, but what the claim rested on — which preparation, which occasion, what it owed him — has not been examined. A thread to be read, not a finding; the claim is stated as the record states it.

desiderata: Riccioli's Almagestum novum (1651) deserves its own record: it is cited here only inside the world-system and crater episodes.

The semi-Tychonic variants: Ursus's scheme of 1588 and Roeslin's of 1597, with Roeslin's comparative plates, are one record since 26 October 2026 (the world systems compared in print); Riccioli's own, and his Almagestum novum, still want a record of their own.

The commemorative record after 1901: the Danish memorials of the 1930s, the monuments before Mortensen (1779–1946) and the commemorations after 1946 are now entered from the Danish museums' records; the quatercentenaries' programmes themselves, the 1971 competition and its plinth, and the Belvedere exhibition of 1971 are not. Vajce's group itself, with Studnička 1901 and the Copernicus year 1973, is entered since 20 October 2026 (the Prague commemoration record).
Kepler's Harmonices mundi (1619) and the third law are not recorded as a separate use of the data; the Science thread jumps from 1609 to 1627.

No online record could be verified for the Týn church's own tomb, for Riccioli's 1651 volumes, for Schjellerup's 1854 memoir, for Bricka's volume of Danske Magazin, or for Zeeberg's two studies; those records carry the citation and no link.

Matiegka's report of 1901 (Bericht über die Untersuchung der Gebeine Tycho Brahe's, Prague 1901) has been read at the page (the house copy, held since 2 October 2026) and the 1901 episode re-cited to it. Still unread: the archaeological report that Matiegka says Herain was preparing for the k. k. Central-Commission in Vienna (printed pp. 4–5); the material in the National Museum's archive that Šimůnek also used; and the joint Herain–Matiegka accounts of 1902, in Czech and in French, that the corpus's bibliographies cite.
Hind's reduction of the comet of 1582 is dated only by the 1846 paper on the comet of 1590; its own place of publication is not recorded here.
The Gingerich citation was resolved by the editor to the 1971 Sky and Telescope article; the compilation's original registry named no work.
Ekdahl's manuscript reports on the 1823-24 excavation, unpublished and un-located in print, would be the only fuller record of what the crypts held when they were opened.
